newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German metal industry deadlocked on sick pay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German metal industry deadlocked on sick pay.

text.p: Germany's largest union and the engineering employers' association on Thursday failed to make any progress towards resolving a bitter dispute over sick pay which has already caused havoc for the country's industry.

Leaders of the IG Metall union and employer group Gesamtmetall emerged from the talks pessimistic on the chances of resolving the dispute and unsure whether it even made sense to set a date for further talks on the matter.

Klaus Zwickel, president of the powerful union, told reporters after the talks that his union remained adamantly opposed to the employers' plans to cut sick pay to 80 percent of the normal wage from 100 percent currently.
"There are absolutely no grounds for optimism," he said, echoing the sentiments of Gesamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe, who told reporters the two sides were still far apart.
At issue is a new federal law which allows companies to reduce sick pay in a bid to cut labour costs to make Germany more attractive and competitive as a production centre.

The unions have made clear in mass walk-outs that they see the legislation as an attack on their free collective bargaining rights, arguing that such benefits were hard won in negotiations and cannot be removed by decree.

Protests involving over 100,000 workers forced Gesametall to retract an original recommendation that its member companies implement the new law without delay. In return, IG Metall promised to suspend its industrial action until further notice.

But the union today set employers a deadline of October 23 by which must they must clarify their intentions once and for all on sick pay. If not, more walkouts and protests in the sector will go ahead as originally planned on October 24.
The latest talks between the two sides failed even to establish whether the sick pay issue should be treated separately or, as Gesamtmetall is demanding, form part of wider 1997 wage negotiations.
Stumpfe said after the meeting that the inclusion of sick pay in the 1997 wage round was an "absolute pre-condition" for fuller negotiations between the two to go ahead.
Gesamtmetall wants discussions to include sick pay, holiday bonuses, employment clauses and 1997 wage increases.

IG Metall, which has consistently argued that the sick pay issue be resolved separately, said it would on Friday inform its regional wage commissions of the Gesamtmetall position and would act on their recommendation.
Responsibility for the regular wage round lies with the regions, and they would have agree to give the leadership full rein to include the 1997 pay demand in their talks.
"We need a positive signal from the wage commissions (on whether discussions can continue," Zwickel said.
Stumpfe said he expected to hear very soon after the weekend whether the union was prepared to re-start discussions, which have been provisionally scheduled for October 21.
The apparent deadlock over sick pay in the engineering industry comes as employers in other sectors face growing opposition as they seek to introduce the cuts.
German chemical union IG Chemie on Thursday demanded immediate negotiations with employers after chemical giant BASF AG's announcement on Tuesday it too planned cuts.
Some 13,000 BASF workers walked off the job on Wednesday in protest at the decision.
